newsitem.title: FRANCE: French unions challenge cutbacks, reform plans.
newsitem.headline: French unions challenge cutbacks, reform plans.

text.p: Strikes disrupted French air traffic and hospitals on Wednesday and unions threatened more widespread action challenging a government drive to push through labour market reforms and cut state spending.
Cockpit crews from British Airways French units Air Liberte and TAT began a 48-hour strike over pay and conditions which unions say will be affected by a merger of the two.
TAT, a domestic airline, said it would guarantee a third of its 90 scheduled flights while Air Liberte, which flies around the world, would maintain two-thirds of its 35 daily flights.
The main claim by pilots and flight engineers was for a two-day rest period every seven days, and 10 rest days per month instead of the current 36 hours each week set by a 1960 decree.
March Rochet, chairman of the two units, said the staff demands would raise costs by 18 percent.

"We can't sustain pilot and flight engineer costs which are too high in France," he told La Tribune daily. "Certainly we need to discuss how to lower costs...but negotiating under pressure is out of the question."

Meanwhile, the government's revocation on Wednesday of a 1937 decree restricting bank hours to allow them to open six days a week was expected to provoke fresh protests by bank staff who fear they will end up working unsocial hours.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said after a cabinet meeting which revised the decree that the move was good for employment.

"It is in the customers' interest and the employee's interest: we will be able to save 10,000 jobs," he said. France's banks are widely regarded as overstaffed and needing to shed jobs to become more competitive.
Junior hospital doctors in the fifth week of a strike over government plans to curb health spending urged all other doctors to join a "health blackout" stoppage of all non-emergency care.

Support for the strike appeared to be gradually eroding after another teaching hospital returned to work on Tuesday, although an opinion poll suggested two-thirds of the public sympathised with the medical interns.
Political commentators said the wide support may reflect the fact that the public was hardly affected by the stoppage.

The dominant Communist-led CGT union called on printers to strike on Thursday to press demands to cut the retirement age to 55. The union said no Paris daily newspapers and only about 20 percent of provincial papers will appear in newsstands.

The protests by bank employees, interns and printers are all part of a test of the conservative government's determination to cut public deficits to qualify for the European Union's planned single currency in 1999.
Truck drivers, threatening to repeat the chaos that swept the country last November, have called a new, indefinite strike for May 5, also to demand a lowering of retirement age to 55.

New stoppages are also expected in coming weeks at the loss-maming, state-owned domestic airline Air France Europe following Easter weekend strikes by ground staff and flight crews which paralysed holiday air traffic.
A court last weekend banned employees of the airline from staging wildcat strikes and said they must give management five days notice.
